message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Doing it yourself the first time is exactly how people learn, and asking questions first is a good sign. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little ledge you can feel with your foot or catch a sock on. It's one of the most visible signs of DIY tiling.

It matters especially for your tiles. **30 × 60 cm porcelain tiles are prone to lippage** because long tiles are often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two ways to avoid it:
- If you stagger them in a brick pattern, offset each row by **a third of the tile's length** (20 cm), **not half**. A half offset puts the high middle of one tile next to the lower end of the next.
- Use **tile levelling clips**. They're cheap plastic clips that pull neighbouring tiles flush while the adhesive sets, and they're very helpful for beginners.

## Grout colour for pale grey tiles

Go for **a mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It hides dirt and footprints far better than white or very pale grout and still looks clean. Avoid white entirely on a floor.

A **stain-resistant or epoxy grout** helps too. Epoxy is harder to work with, so for a first job a good stain-resistant cement grout plus a grout sealer is a sensible middle ground.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** The toilet should sit on top of the finished tiles. That gives a neat, continuous floor that's easier to clean, avoids fiddly cuts around the toilet base, and makes it easy to replace the toilet later. Just make sure the waste pipe and connections will work at the new floor height.

## How many boxes?

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).**

- Floor area: 2.4 m × 1.8 m = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 m × 0.6 m = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, rounded up to **27 tiles**
- Boxes: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.375, so **4 boxes**

That gives you 32 tiles, about **8 spare**, which is a good thing:
- **Cuts around the toilet pipe and doorway, and walls that aren't quite square**, use more tiles than the simple maths suggests, especially for a first-timer.
- **Keep a few spares.** If one cracks in five years, you'll need a matching tile.
- **Check that all boxes share the same batch number.** Colour can vary between production runs.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [names], just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there may be some noise from about [9am] for a couple of hours. Thank you so much for your patience — we know the skip's been on the drive for a while too, and it should be gone soon! Do shout if there's a time that's particularly bad for you.

If you get on well, a small box of biscuits delivered with it tends to go down very well.

## Three tips for a beginner

1. **Preparation decides the result.** The subfloor has to be **flat, rigid and clean**. Any flex, bump or dip will show up as cracked tiles or lippage. If it's a timber floor, it may need overboarding with tile backer board or ply first. Spend time here, as it's the step videos rush past.
2. **Dry-lay before you mix any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers to plan where the cuts fall. Aim for cut tiles at the edges that are at least half a tile wide, not thin slivers, and keep full tiles in the most visible areas, such as the doorway. Start from the centre line, not from a wall, because walls are rarely straight.
3. **Check adhesive coverage and work in small areas.** Use the right notched trowel (the tile shop can advise). For large tiles, also spread a thin layer of adhesive on the back of each tile. Lift the first tile or two back up to check the back is fully covered, because gaps underneath lead to cracks. Mix only as much adhesive as you can use in about 20–30 minutes, and keep wiping excess out of the joints as you go.

A practical bonus: **hire or buy a wet tile cutter** for porcelain. It makes clean cuts much easier, and it's where most of that Saturday noise will come from.

You'll be fine. Take it slowly, check that everything is level as you go, and don't be afraid to lift a tile and relay it.
